context:
When each of the four identical sp3 hybrid orbitals of a carbon atom overlaps with the 1s orbital of a hydrogen atom, four identical C–H bonds are formed and methane results. Each C–H bond in methane has a strength of 439 kJ/mol (105 kcal/mol) and a length of 109 pm. Because the four bonds have a specific geometry, we also can define a property called the bond angle. The angle formed by each H–C–H is 109.5°, the so-called tetrahedral angle. Methane thus has the structure shown in the figure.

The structure of methane, showing its 109.5° bond angles.

The space-filling model, wedge-dash structure, and ball and stick model of methane. The bond length between C-H is 109 pm, and the bond angle of H-C-H is 109.5 degrees.
caption: The structure of methane, showing its 109.5° bond angles.
source: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, chapter 1: Structure and Bonding
input prompt: This figure renders a single methane molecule three ways in one row, moving from a solid-volume picture to a measured structural drawing to an open skeleton. At the left is a space-filling model in which four large off-white hydrogen spheres crowd around a dark gray carbon that is barely visible between them, the spheres touching and flattening against one another. In the center is a structural drawing: the central "C" joins an "H" directly above, an "H" at the left, and an "H" at the right by plain black lines, and a fourth "H" below by a heavy black wedge. A magenta double-headed curved arrow sweeps between two dashed magenta rays that extend the upward and left-hand bonds, labeled "Bond angle 109.5º". Short magenta dashed lines run rightward from the upper hydrogen and from the carbon to a vertical double arrow labeled "Bond length 109 pm". At the right is a ball-and-stick model with the dark gray carbon at the center and four pale hydrogen spheres held out on thin pale blue rods. Showing one molecule in three styles lets the reader attach the two measurements to a shape also seen as filled volume, fixing the tetrahedral geometry that results when four equivalent hybrid orbitals on carbon overlap with hydrogen orbitals.
interactions:
- Toggle representation style: space-filling, structural, and ball-and-stick views highlight the same methane molecule, showing how each representation emphasizes size, angles, or connectivity.
- Slider for dragging one hydrogen around the carbon; the structural drawing and model morph while the bond-angle readout updates toward 109.5 degrees, making the connection between four equivalent C-H bonds and tetrahedral spacing visible.

context:
Despite what we’ve just said, we actually don’t observe perfectly free rotation in ethane. Experiments show that there is a small (12 kJ/mol; 2.9 kcal/mol) barrier to rotation and that some conformations are more stable than others. The lowest-energy, most stable conformation is the one in which all six C–H bonds are as far away from one another as possible—staggered when viewed end-on in a Newman projection. The highest-energy, least stable conformation is the one in which the six C–H bonds are as close as possible—eclipsed in a Newman projection. At any given instant, about 99% of ethane molecules have an approximately staggered conformation and only about 1% are near the eclipsed conformation.

Staggered conformation of ethane undergoes rotation of rear carbon 60 degrees to form eclipsed conformation of ethane.

The extra 12 kJ/mol of energy present in the eclipsed conformation of ethane is called torsional strain. Its cause has been the subject of controversy, but the major factor is an interaction between C–H bonding orbitals on one carbon and antibonding orbitals on the adjacent carbon, which stabilizes the staggered conformation relative to the eclipsed one. Because a total strain of 12 kJ/mol arises from three equal hydrogen–hydrogen eclipsing interactions, we can assign a value of approximately 4.0 kJ/mol (1.0 kcal/mol) to each single interaction. The barrier to rotation that results can be represented on a graph of potential energy versus degree of rotation, in which the angle between C–H bonds on the front and back carbons as viewed end-on (the dihedral angle) goes full circle from 0 to 360°. Energy minima occur at staggered conformations, and energy maxima occur at eclipsed conformations, as shown in the figure.
source: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, chapter 3: Organic Compounds: Alkanes and Their Stereochemistry
input prompt: This figure compares two conformations of ethane, each shown as a Newman projection paired with a ball-and-stick model, with a reaction-style arrow between them. On the left, the Newman projection draws the front carbon as a dot at the center of a circle with three heavy bonds radiating up, down-left, and down-right to hydrogens lettered in green, while the rear carbon is the circle itself with three thinner bonds emerging at the left, right, and bottom to hydrogens lettered in magenta, so the two sets alternate evenly. Its ball-and-stick model, viewed end-on, shows a dark gray carbon ringed by three green and three red spheres in alternating positions. The horizontal arrow between the halves is labeled "Rotate rear carbon 60°". On the right, the projection shows each front bond lying directly over a rear bond, so the green and magenta hydrogens appear in overlapping pairs, and three curly braces, one at each pair, are each labeled "4.0 kJ/mol". The matching model now shows the green and red spheres in coincident pairs. Bold labels read "Ethane—staggered conformation" and "Ethane—eclipsed conformation". Setting the two projections side by side makes the hydrogen spacing the thing being compared, and the three equal energy labels partition the rotational barrier into individual eclipsing interactions.
interactions:
- Slider for rotating the rear carbon from 0 to 60 degrees; the Newman projection and ball-and-stick model update continuously from staggered to eclipsed, making torsional alignment the source of the conformational change.
- Click for highlighting one eclipsed H-H pair; its brace and 4.0 kJ/mol label brighten along with the overlapping hydrogens, clarifying how three identical interactions add to the rotational barrier.

context:
How can the hybrid-orbital model of bonding account for the large distortion of bond angles from the normal 109° tetrahedral value to 60° in cyclopropane? The answer is that cyclopropane has bent bonds. In an unstrained alkane, maximum bonding is achieved when two atoms have their overlapping orbitals pointing directly toward each other. In cyclopropane, though, the orbitals can’t point directly toward each other; instead, they overlap at a slight angle. The result is that cyclopropane bonds are weaker and more reactive than typical alkane bonds—255 kJ/mol (61 kcal/mol) for a C−C bond in cyclopropane versus 370 kJ/mol (88 kcal/mol) for a C−C bond in open-chain propane.

Orbital representations show typical alkane C-C bonds with 109 degrees angle and typical bent cyclopropane C-C bonds.
source: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, chapter 4: Organic Compounds: Cycloalkanes and Their Stereochemistry
input prompt: This figure places two orbital-overlap drawings side by side to contrast the bonding geometry of an open chain with that of a three-membered ring. On the left, three carbons lettered "C" sit at the ends and apex of a shallow V, with black dashed lines drawn through them marking the straight paths from nucleus to nucleus. Pink lobes of electron density project from each carbon along those dashed lines and meet head-on midway between neighboring atoms, the overlap regions shaded a deeper rose. A magenta double-headed arc spans the angle at the central carbon, labeled "109°". On the right, three carbons lettered "C" occupy the corners of a triangle. Dashed lines again mark the internuclear directions, but the pink lobes now emerge tilted away from them, so each pair meets outside the edge of the triangle rather than along the line joining the two carbons, leaving the interior open. Bold captions read "Typical alkane C−C bonds" and "Typical bent cyclopropane C−C bonds". Drawing the internuclear lines in both panels lets the reader compare where the lobes point against where the atoms actually lie, which accounts for why a ring squeezed to a 60 degree angle forms curved, poorly overlapped bonds that are weaker and more reactive than ordinary ones.
interactions:
- Slider for decreasing the C-C-C angle from a typical alkane value toward 60 degrees; the pink orbital lobes bend away from the dashed internuclear lines and the overlap patch shifts outward, showing why cyclopropane bonds are curved and strained.
- Toggle between Typical alkane C-C bonds and Typical bent cyclopropane C-C bonds; the same dashed nucleus-to-nucleus guides remain visible, making head-on overlap versus off-axis overlap the comparison to track.

context:
Cyclohexane adopts a strain-free, three-dimensional shape that is called a chair conformation because of its similarity to a lounge chair, with a back, seat, and footrest (the figure). Chair cyclohexane has neither angle strain nor torsional strain—all C−C−C bond angles are near the 109° tetrahedral value, and all neighboring C−H bonds are staggered.

The strain-free chair conformation of cyclohexane. All C−C−C bond angles are 111.5°, close to the ideal 109° tetrahedral angle, and all neighboring C−H bonds are staggered.

The ball and stick model, chair conformation, and Newman projection of cyclohexane. The carbon atoms are numbered in chair conformation and Newman projection.

The easiest way to visualize chair cyclohexane is to build a molecular model if you have access to a model kit, or alternatively to explore with one of the many computer-based modeling programs you may have access to.
caption: The strain-free chair conformation of cyclohexane. All C−C−C bond angles are 111.5°, close to the ideal 109° tetrahedral angle, and all neighboring C−H bonds are staggered.
source: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, chapter 4: Organic Compounds: Cycloalkanes and Their Stereochemistry
input prompt: This figure shows cyclohexane in its chair form through three labeled panels, (a), (b), and (c). Panel (a) is a ball-and-stick model of the six-membered ring: six dark gray carbon spheres joined by pale rods trace a shape that rises at one end and dips at the other, each carbon carrying two off-white hydrogen spheres. Panel (b) redraws the same ring as a line structure with the near bonds bolded to signal depth, its carbons numbered 1 through 6 in magenta and its hydrogens lettered in magenta, green, blue, and black. Two drawn eyes at the right, marked "Observer", send magenta dashed sightlines to carbon 1 and to carbon 5. Panel (c) is the corresponding Newman projection: two circles, each with a front carbon dot and three bonds, are joined at the top and bottom by groups written "CH2", with the front atoms numbered 1 and 5 and the surrounding hydrogens numbered 2, 3, 4, and 6 in matching colors. Carrying the same numbering and hydrogen colors through all three panels lets the reader map any position on the model onto the corresponding position in the end-on view. Together the panels demonstrate that the chair shape holds its bond angles near the tetrahedral value while keeping every pair of neighboring C-H bonds staggered, leaving the ring free of strain.
interactions:
- Click for selecting carbon 1 or carbon 5 in the line drawing; the matching front carbon, hydrogens, and CH2 connectors highlight in the Newman projection, clarifying how positions transfer between representations.
- Toggle among ball-and-stick, line structure, and Newman projection panels; the ball-and-stick view establishes the 3D chair shape, while the line structure and Newman projection carry the matching hydrogen colors used to track staggered neighboring C-H bonds.

context:
As shown in the figure, each carbon atom in chair cyclohexane has one axial and one equatorial hydrogen. Furthermore, each side of the ring has three axial and three equatorial hydrogens in an alternating arrangement. For example, if the top side of the ring has axial hydrogens on carbons 1, 3, and 5, then it has equatorial hydrogens on carbons 2, 4, and 6. The reverse is true for the bottom side: carbons 1, 3, and 5 have equatorial hydrogens, but carbons 2, 4, and 6 have axial hydrogens (the figure).

Alternating axial and equatorial positions in chair cyclohexane, looking directly down the ring axis. Each carbon atom has one axial and one equatorial position, and each face has alternating axial and equatorial positions.

The space-filling model and ball and stick model of cyclohexane with alternate axial and equatorial positions, represented by red and blue spheres, respectively.

Note that we haven’t used the words cis and trans in this discussion of cyclohexane conformation. Two hydrogens on the same side of the ring are always cis, regardless of whether they’re axial or equatorial and regardless of whether they’re adjacent. Similarly, two hydrogens on opposite sides of the ring are always trans.
caption: Alternating axial and equatorial positions in chair cyclohexane, looking directly down the ring axis. Each carbon atom has one axial and one equatorial position, and each face has alternating axial and equatorial positions.
source: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, chapter 4: Organic Compounds: Cycloalkanes and Their Stereochemistry
input prompt: This figure looks straight down the axis of a chair-form cyclohexane ring in two matched models that color-code the two kinds of hydrogen position. On the left is a space-filling model: a compact dark gray core of ring carbons is surrounded by six large red spheres and six large blue spheres packed against one another, the red ones sitting toward the center of the disc and the blue ones fanning outward around the rim, the two colors alternating as the eye travels around the ring. A magenta arrow at the upper left points to a red sphere and is labeled "Axial"; a blue arrow at the top points to a blue sphere and is labeled "Equatorial". On the right the same view appears as a ball-and-stick model, the six dark gray carbons forming a hexagonal outline, with red spheres projecting from alternating carbons and blue spheres held outward from every carbon on thin pale rods. Separating the two positions by color rather than by perspective lets the reader count them directly, establishing that each ring carbon bears exactly one axial and one equatorial hydrogen and that each face carries three of each in alternating order.
interactions:
- Click for selecting any ring carbon in the ball-and-stick model; its paired axial and equatorial hydrogens brighten together, clarifying that the two positions coexist on each carbon rather than belonging to separate molecules.
- Toggle axial only, equatorial only, and both: red and blue hydrogens fade in and out on both models, making the one-axial-one-equatorial pattern at every ring carbon countable.

context:
What causes molecular handedness? Look at generalized molecules of the type CH3X, CH2XY, and CHXYZ shown in the figure. On the left are three molecules, and on the right are their images reflected in a mirror. The CH3X and CH2XY molecules are identical to their mirror images and thus are not handed. If you make a molecular model of each molecule and its mirror image, you find that you can superimpose one on the other so that all atoms coincide. The CHXYZ molecule, by contrast, is not identical to its mirror image. You can’t superimpose a model of this molecule on a model of its mirror image for the same reason that you can’t superimpose a left hand on a right hand: they simply aren’t the same.

Tetrahedral carbon atoms and their mirror images. Molecules of the type CH3X and CH2XY are identical to their mirror images, but a molecule of the type CHXYZ is not. A CHXYZ molecule is related to its mirror image in the same way a right hand is related to a left hand.

The figure shows condensed formulas, structures, and ball-and-stick models of C H 3 X, C H 2 X Y, and C H X Y Z along with their mirror images.

A molecule that is not identical to its mirror image is a kind of stereoisomer (another section) called an enantiomer (e-nan-tee-oh-mer, from the Greek enantio, meaning “opposite”). Enantiomers are related to each other as a right hand is related to a left hand and result whenever a tetrahedral carbon is bonded to four different substituents (one need not be H). For example, lactic acid (2-hydroxypropanoic acid) exists as a pair of enantiomers because there are four different groups (−H, −OH, −CH3, −CO2H) bonded to the central carbon atom. The enantiomers are called (+)-lactic acid and (−)-lactic acid. Both are found in sour milk, but only the (+) enantiomer occurs in muscle tissue.
caption: Tetrahedral carbon atoms and their mirror images. Molecules of the type CH3X and CH2XY are identical to their mirror images, but a molecule of the type CHXYZ is not. A CHXYZ molecule is related to its mirror image in the same way a right hand is related to a left hand.
source: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, chapter 5: Stereochemistry at Tetrahedral Centers
input prompt: This figure arranges three generalized carbon compounds in three rows and reflects each one in a drawn mirror. Each row begins at the left with a condensed formula written in colored letters, "CH3X", "CH2XY", and "CHXYZ", with X in magenta, Y in blue, and Z in gold. Next comes a structural drawing in which a central "C" bonds upward by a plain line, to the left and right by plain lines, and downward by a heavy wedge; the four attached labels are X, H, H and H in the top row, X, H, Y and H in the middle row, and X, H, Y and Z in the bottom row. Third in each row is a ball-and-stick model with a dark gray carbon carrying a red sphere above and green, blue, or yellow spheres below according to the substituents named. At the right stands a tall pale blue rectangular pane with a highlight streak, representing a mirror, and behind it each model appears again as its reflection, with the substituent spheres reversed left to right. Repeating the same three columns down every row isolates substitution pattern as the only variable, so the reader can test each reflection against its original. The layout introduces the condition under which a tetrahedral carbon and its mirror image cease to be superimposable, the structural basis of molecular handedness.
interactions:
- Drag for moving each mirror-image model onto its original; CH3X and CH2XY can be aligned by rotation while CHXYZ leaves mismatched colored substituents, making superimposability the test for chirality.
- Toggle between CH3X, CH2XY, and CHXYZ rows; the mirror pane and color scheme remain fixed while only substituent variety changes, clarifying why four different groups at tetrahedral carbon create handedness.

context:
The angle of rotation can be measured with an instrument called a polarimeter, represented in the figure. A solution of optically active organic molecules is placed in a sample tube, plane-polarized light is passed through the tube, and rotation of the polarization plane occurs. The light then goes through a second polarizer called the analyzer. By rotating the analyzer until the light passes through it, we can find the new plane of polarization and can tell to what extent rotation has occurred.

Schematic representation of a polarimeter. Plane-polarized light passes through a solution of optically active molecules, which rotate the plane of polarization.

Schematic representation of a polarimeter. Unpolarized light from light source passes through polarizer, followed by polarized light, sample tube containing organic molecules, analyzer, and observer.

In addition to determining the extent of rotation, we can also find the direction. From the vantage point of the observer looking directly at the analyzer, some optically active molecules rotate polarized light to the left (counterclockwise) and are said to be levorotatory, whereas others rotate polarized light to the right (clockwise) and are said to be dextrorotatory. By convention, rotation to the left is given a minus sign (−) and rotation to the right is given a plus sign (+). (−)-Morphine, for example, is levorotatory, and (+)-sucrose is dextrorotatory.
caption: Schematic representation of a polarimeter. Plane-polarized light passes through a solution of optically active molecules, which rotate the plane of polarization.
source: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, chapter 5: Stereochemistry at Tetrahedral Centers
input prompt: This figure is a schematic drawing of a polarimeter, laid out as a single optical path running left to right in perspective. At the far left a lit incandescent bulb sits in a socket inside a yellow glow, labeled "Light source", and short red double-headed arrows pointing in many directions emerge from it beneath the label "Unpolarized light". The beam is drawn as a flat pale yellow ribbon that passes through a circular disc with fine vertical striping, labeled "Polarizer", after which the red arrows all lie in a single vertical plane under the label "Polarized light". The ribbon then runs through a horizontal cylinder with a small filling stub on top, drawn with rounded ends and labeled "Sample tube containing organic molecules"; the red arrows inside progressively tip away from vertical as they move along the tube. Beyond the tube the beam meets a second striped disc labeled "Analyzer" and continues to the right, where a heavy red double-headed arrow lies at a slant. A vertical dashed reference line and a curved arrow mark the angle between the two, labeled with the Greek letter alpha, and a drawn eye at the right edge is labeled "Observer". Tracking one ribbon of light through every component makes the tilt of the arrows the quantity to follow. The arrangement shows how the rotation an optically active sample imposes on the plane of polarization is measured.
interactions:
- Slider for rotating the analyzer disc; the outgoing red polarization arrow and measured alpha angle update with the disc, showing how the observer finds the sample-imposed rotation.
- Slider for changing sample optical activity from zero to a larger positive or negative value; the red arrows inside the tube progressively twist and the final beam angle follows, making rotation of plane-polarized light depend on the organic sample.
- Animation for sending pulses of light from source through polarizer, sample tube, and analyzer; the arrows change from many directions to one plane and then to a tilted plane, clarifying each component's role along the optical path.

context:
The 2R,3S and 2S,3R structures are identical because the molecule has a plane of symmetry and is therefore achiral. The symmetry plane cuts through the C2–C3 bond, making one half of the molecule a mirror image of the other half (the figure). Because of the plane of symmetry, the molecule is achiral, despite the fact that it has two chirality centers. Such compounds, which are achiral, yet contain chirality centers, are called meso compounds (me-zo). Thus, tartaric acid exists in three stereoisomeric forms: two enantiomers and one meso form.

A symmetry plane through the C2–C3 bond of meso-tartaric acid makes the molecule achiral.

The wedge-dash structure and ball-and-stick model of tartaric acid. C2 and C3 have a horizontal symmetry plane.

Some physical properties of the three stereoisomers are listed in the table. The (+)- and (−)-tartaric acids have identical melting points, solubilities, and densities, but they differ in the sign of their rotation of plane-polarized light. The meso isomer, by contrast, is diastereomeric with the (+) and (−) forms. It has no mirror-image relationship to (+)- and (−)-tartaric acids, is a different compound altogether, and thus has different physical properties.
caption: A symmetry plane through the C2–C3 bond of meso-tartaric acid makes the molecule achiral.
source: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, chapter 5: Stereochemistry at Tetrahedral Centers
input prompt: This figure pairs a flat structural drawing with a three-dimensional model of the same molecule, both cut by a horizontal plane. On the left, two carbons lettered "C" sit one above the other, joined by a vertical bond. The upper carbon bears an "H" above it on a dashed bond, an "HO" group at the left in magenta on a bold wedge, and a "CO2H" group at the right in green. The lower carbon repeats that arrangement flipped vertically: "HO" again at the left and "CO2H" at the right, but its "H" now points downward on a dashed bond. A pale blue parallelogram drawn edge-on slices horizontally between the two carbons, labeled "Symmetry plane". On the right the molecule appears as a ball-and-stick model, two dark gray carbons stacked vertically, each carrying a small blue sphere, a red oxygen with a second red sphere beyond it, and a branching green group, with an identical pale blue plane passing between them. Running the plane through both depictions asks the reader to check one half against the other. Because the halves are reflections, the molecule proves superimposable on its own mirror image despite having two chirality centers, the situation that defines a meso compound.
interactions:
- Click for selecting an HO, H, or CO2H group on one stereocenter; the reflected counterpart on the other stereocenter highlights across the plane, clarifying why the two halves cancel molecular handedness.
- Toggle between structure-only, model-only, and overlay views of the symmetry plane; the pale plane persists across representations, showing that the same internal reflection explains achirality despite two chirality centers.

context:
Although essentially free rotation around single bonds is possible (another section), the same is not true of double bonds. For rotation to occur around a double bond, the π bond must break and re-form (the figure). Thus, the barrier to double-bond rotation must be at least as great as the strength of the π bond itself, an estimated 350 kJ/mol (84 kcal/mol). Recall that the barrier to bond rotation in ethane is only 12 kJ/mol.

The π bond must break for rotation to take place around a carbon–carbon double bond.

An orbital diagram with two parallel p orbitals before rotation. After rotation the p orbitals are perpendicular, which breaks the double bond.

The lack of rotation around carbon–carbon double bonds is of more than just theoretical interest; it also has chemical consequences. Imagine the situation for a disubstituted alkene such as 2-butene. (Disubstituted means that two substituents other than hydrogen are bonded to the double-bond carbons.) The two methyl groups in 2-butene can either be on the same side of the double bond or on opposite sides, a situation similar to that in disubstituted cycloalkanes (another section).
caption: The π bond must break for rotation to take place around a carbon–carbon double bond.
source: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, chapter 7: Alkenes: Structure and Reactivity
input prompt: This figure shows two orbital drawings of a carbon-carbon double bond separated by a labeled arrow, before and after a twist. On the left, two carbons lettered "C" are stacked diagonally, each drawn with a pink lobe above and a blue lobe below, the lobes tapering to points at the carbon and each pink lobe carrying a small black dot. The two sets are parallel, and thin straight lines run along the outer edges of the upper pink pair and the lower blue pair to show that the lobes line up so their broad faces overlap sideways; short black bars and dashed lines at each carbon mark the remaining bonds and the plane they occupy. A horizontal arrow across the middle is labeled "rotate 90°". On the right the lower carbon is unchanged, but the upper one has been turned so its pink lobe points toward the viewer at the left and its blue lobe away at the right, leaving the two pairs crossing at right angles instead of running parallel. Bold labels beneath read "π bond (p orbitals are parallel)" and "Broken π bond after rotation (p orbitals are perpendicular)". Setting the aligned lobes against the crossed ones makes sideways overlap the thing to watch, explaining why twisting such a bond costs the full strength of the pi bond and so does not happen freely.
interactions:
- Slider for rotating the upper carbon from 0 to 90 degrees; the p orbitals move from parallel overlap to perpendicular separation while an overlap or pi-bond-strength indicator falls, making pi-bond breaking the cost of rotation.
- Toggle between aligned p orbitals and broken pi bond after rotation; the same carbon framework remains in place while the orbital faces switch orientation, clarifying that sideways overlap exists only when the p orbitals are parallel.

context:
As shown in the figure, the SN2 reaction occurs when an electron pair on the nucleophile Nu:– forces out the group X:–, which takes with it the electron pair from the former C–X bond. This occurs through a transition state in which the new Nu–C bond is partially formed at the same time that the old C–X bond is partially broken and in which the negative charge is shared by both the incoming nucleophile and the outgoing halide ion. The transition state for this inversion has the remaining three bonds to carbon in a planar arrangement (the figure).

The transition state of an SN2 reaction has a planar arrangement of the carbon atom and the remaining three groups. Electrostatic potential maps show that negative charge is delocalized in the transition state.

The figure shows the S N 2 reaction along with their ball-and-stick model in electrostatic potential maps. Tertiary alkyl halide and substituted compound are tetrahedral, while transition state is planar.

The mechanism proposed by Hughes and Ingold is fully consistent with experimental results, explaining both stereochemical and kinetic data. Thus, the requirement for a backside approach of the entering nucleophile (180° away from the departing X group) causes the stereochemistry of the substrate to invert, much like an umbrella turning inside-out in the wind. The Hughes–Ingold mechanism also explains why second-order kinetics are observed: the SN2 reaction occurs in a single step that involves both alkyl halide and nucleophile. Two molecules are involved in the step whose rate is measured.
caption: The transition state of an SN2 reaction has a planar arrangement of the carbon atom and the remaining three groups. Electrostatic potential maps show that negative charge is delocalized in the transition state.
source: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, chapter 11: Reactions of Alkyl Halides: Nucleophilic Substitutions and Eliminations
input prompt: This figure pairs a three-step reaction scheme with electrostatic potential maps to follow an SN2 substitution, arranged in three stacked rows with the maps on the left and the structures on the right. The top row writes Nu:- in magenta, a plus sign, and a tetrahedral carbon drawn with one bold wedge, one hashed bond, and two plain bonds, joined to a magenta X; alongside it the maps show the free nucleophile as an isolated deep red sphere and the alkyl halide as a two-lobed surface labeled "Tetrahedral" whose halide end is also red. A downward arrow leads to the middle row, where the transition state sits inside square brackets with Nu at the left and X at the right, each carrying a magenta delta- and each tied to the central carbon by a dotted line while the remaining three bonds to that carbon lie in a plane; its map is a wide, symmetric three-lobed surface labeled "Planar", red at both ends and green and yellow across the middle. A second arrow reaches the product row, Nu-C with the wedge and hash now reversed, plus X:-, mapped as a lobed Nu-bearing surface labeled "Tetrahedral" beside a separate red halide sphere. Read down the column, the color scale tracks negative charge leaving the nucleophile, spreading over both ends of the planar species, and settling on the departing halide. The layout supports a single-step mechanism in which backside attack 180 degrees from the leaving group turns the carbon's substituents inside out.
interactions: - Slider for reaction progress: drag from reactants through the bracketed transition state to products, and the geometry morphs from tetrahedral to planar and back while the red electrostatic potential shifts from nucleophile to both ends to leaving group, making charge delocalization during one-step SN2 substitution clear.

context:
The operation of a basic NMR spectrometer is illustrated in the figure. An organic sample is dissolved in a suitable solvent (usually deuteriochloroform, CDCl3, which has no hydrogens) and placed in a thin glass tube between the poles of a magnet. The strong magnetic field causes the 1H and 13C nuclei in the molecule to align in one of the two possible orientations, and the sample is irradiated with rf energy. If the frequency of the rf irradiation is held constant and the strength of the applied magnetic field is varied, each nucleus comes into resonance at a slightly different field strength. A sensitive detector monitors the absorption of rf energy, and its electronic signal is then amplified and displayed as a peak.

Schematic operation of a basic NMR spectrometer. A thin glass tube containing the sample solution is placed between the poles of a strong magnet and irradiated with rf energy.

Schematic diagram of spectrometer shows sample in tube placed between south and north poles. Tube connects to radiofrequency generator (left) and detector and amplifier (right), which further connects to monitor.

NMR spectroscopy differs from IR spectroscopy (another section–another section) in that the timescales of the two techniques are quite different. The absorption of infrared energy by a molecule giving rise to a change in vibrational amplitude is an essentially instantaneous process (about 10–13 s), but the NMR process is much slower (about 10–3 s). This difference in timescales between IR and NMR spectroscopy is analogous to the difference between cameras operating at very fast and very slow shutter speeds. The fast camera (IR) takes an instantaneous picture and freezes the action. If two rapidly interconverting species are present, IR spectroscopy records the spectrum of both. The slow camera (NMR), however, takes a blurred, time-averaged picture. If two species interconverting faster than 103 times per second are present in a sample, NMR records only a single, averaged spectrum, rather than separate spectra of the two discrete species.
caption: Schematic operation of a basic NMR spectrometer. A thin glass tube containing the sample solution is placed between the poles of a strong magnet and irradiated with rf energy.
source: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, chapter 13: Structure Determination: Nuclear Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy
input prompt: This figure is a perspective pictorial schematic of a basic NMR spectrometer, laying out sample, magnet, and signal path in one view. Because they are like soaps in having a long, nonpolar hydrocarbon tail bound to a polar ionic head, phospholipids in the cell membrane organize into a lipid bilayer about 5.0 nm (50 Å) thick. As shown in the figure, the nonpolar tails aggregate in the center of the bilayer in much the same way that soap tails aggregate in the center of a micelle. This bilayer serves as an effective barrier to the passage of water, ions, and other components into and out of cells.

Following formation of the polymerase–promoter complex, several turns of the DNA double helix untwist, forming a bubble and exposing 14 or so base pairs of the two strands. Appropriate ribonucleotides then line up by hydrogen-bonding to their complementary bases on DNA, bond formation occurs in the 5′ → 3′ direction, the RNA polymerase moves along the DNA chain, and the growing RNA molecule unwinds from DNA (the figure). At any one time, about 12 base pairs of the growing RNA remain hydrogen-bonded to the DNA template.

Biosynthesis of RNA using a DNA segment as a template.

Several turns of deoxyribonucleic acid double helix unwind exposing bases of the two strands. Ribonucleotides line up such that hydrogen bonds form in 5-prime to 3-prime direction.

Unlike what happens in DNA replication, where both strands are copied, only one of the two DNA strands is transcribed into mRNA. The DNA strand that contains the gene is often called the sense strand, or coding strand, and the DNA strand that gets transcribed to give RNA is called the antisense strand, or noncoding strand. Because the sense strand and the antisense strand in DNA are complementary, and because the DNA antisense strand and the newly formed RNA strand are also complementary, the RNA molecule produced during transcription is a copy of the DNA sense strand. That is, the complement of the complement is the same as the original. The only difference is that the RNA molecule has a U everywhere that the DNA sense strand has a T.
caption: Biosynthesis of RNA using a DNA segment as a template.
source: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, chapter 28: Biomolecules: Nucleic Acids

A red-black tree is a binary search tree with one extra bit of storage per node: its color, which can be either RED or BLACK. By constraining the node colors on any simple path from the root to a leaf, red-black trees ensure that no such path is more than twice as long as any other, so that the tree is approximately balanced. Each node of the tree now contains the attributes color, key, left, right, and p. If a child or the parent of a node does not exist, the corresponding pointer attribute of the node contains the value NIL. We shall regard these NILs as being pointers to leaves (external nodes) of the binary search tree and the normal, key-bearing nodes as being internal nodes of the tree. A red-black tree is a binary tree that satisfies the following red-black properties: 1. Every node is either red or black. 2. The root is black. 3. Every leaf (NIL) is black. 4. If a node is red, then both its children are black. 5. For each node, all simple paths from the node to descendant leaves contain the same number of black nodes. Figure 13.1(a) shows an example of a red-black tree.
As a matter of convenience in dealing with boundary conditions in red-black
tree code, we use a single sentinel to represent NIL (see page 238). For a red-black
tree T , the sentinel T:nil is an object with the same attributes as an ordinary node
in the tree. Its color attribute is BLACK, and its other attributes—p, left, right,
and key—can take on arbitrary values. As Figure 13.1(b) shows, all pointers to NIL
are replaced by pointers to the sentinel T:nil.
We use the sentinel so that we can treat a NIL child of a node x as an ordinary
node whose parent is x. Although we instead could add a distinct sentinel node
for each NIL in the tree, so that the parent of each NIL is well defined, that approach would waste space. Instead, we use the one sentinel T:nil to represent all
the NILs—all leaves and the root’s parent. The values of the attributes p, left, right,
and key of the sentinel are immaterial, although we may set them during the course
of a procedure for our convenience.
We generally confine our interest to the internal nodes of a red-black tree, since
they hold the key values. In the remainder of this chapter, we omit the leaves when
we draw red-black trees, as shown in Figure 13.1(c).

context: The search-tree operations TREE-INSERT and TREE-DELETE, when run on a redblack tree with n keys, take O.lg n/ time. Because they modify the tree, the result may violate the red-black properties enumerated in Section 13.1. To restore these properties, we must change the colors of some of the nodes in the tree and also change the pointer structure. We change the pointer structure through rotation, which is a local operation in a search tree that preserves the binary-search-tree property. Figure 13.2 shows the two kinds of rotations: left rotations and right rotations. When we do a left rotation on a node x, we assume that its right child y is not T:nil; x may be any node in the tree whose right child is not T:nil. The left rotation “pivots” around the link from x to y. It makes y the new root of the subtree, with x as y’s left child and y’s left child as x’s right child.

The operation LEFT-ROTATE.T; x/ transforms the configuration of the two nodes on the right into the configuration on the left by changing a constant number of pointers. A rotation operation preserves the binary-search-tree property: the keys in ˛ precede x:key, which precedes the keys in ˇ, which precede y:key, which precedes the keys in .

Part (a) of the figure shows T .n/, which we expand in part (b) into an equivalent tree representing the recurrence. The cn term is the root (the cost incurred at the top level of recursion), and the two subtrees of the root are the two smaller recurrences T .n=2/. Part (c) shows this process carried one step further by expanding T .n=2/. The cost incurred at each of the two subnodes at the second level of recursion is cn=2. We continue expanding each node in the tree by breaking it into its constituent parts as determined by the recurrence, until the problem sizes get down to 1, each with a cost of c. Part (d) shows the resulting recursion tree. Next, we add the costs across each level of the tree. The top level has total cost cn, the next level down has total cost c.n=2/ C c.n=2/ D cn, the level after that has total cost c.n=4/Cc.n=4/Cc.n=4/Cc.n=4/ D cn, and so on. In general, the level i below the top has 2 i nodes, each contributing a cost of c.n=2i /, so that the ith level below the top has total cost 2 i c.n=2i / D cn. The bottom level has n nodes, each contributing a cost of c, for a total cost of cn. The total number of levels of the recursion tree in Figure 2.5 is lg n C 1, where n is the number of leaves, corresponding to the input size. An informal inductive argument justifies this claim. The base case occurs when n D 1, in which case the tree has only one level. Since lg 1 D 0, we have that lg n C 1 gives the correct number of levels. Now assume as an inductive hypothesis that the number of levels of a recursion tree with 2 i leaves is lg 2 i C 1 D i C 1 (since for any value of i, we have that lg 2 i D i). Because we are assuming that the input size is a power of 2, the next input size to consider is 2 iC1 . A tree with n D 2 iC1 leaves has one more level than a tree with 2 i leaves, and so the total number of levels is .i C 1/ C 1 D lg 2 iC1 C 1. To compute the total cost represented by the recurrence (2.2), we simply add up the costs of all the levels. The recursion tree has lg n C 1 levels, each costing cn, for a total cost of cn.lg n C 1/ D cn lg n C cn. Ignoring the low-order term and the constant c gives the desired result of ‚.n lg n/.

context: The maximum-bipartite-matching problem Given an undirected graph G D .V; E/, a matching is a subset of edges M _x0012_ E such that for all vertices _x0017_ 2 V , at most one edge of M is incident on _x0017_. We say that a vertex _x0017_ 2 V is matched by the matching M if some edge in M is incident on _x0017_; otherwise, _x0017_ is unmatched. A maximum matching is a matching of maximum cardinality, that is, a matching M such that for any matching M0 , we have jMj _x0015_ jM0 j. In this section, we shall restrict our attention to finding maximum matchings in bipartite graphs: graphs in which the vertex set can be partitioned into V D L [ R, where L and R are disjoint and all edges in E go between L and R. We further assume that every vertex in V has at least one incident edge. Figure 26.8 illustrates the notion of a matching in a bipartite graph. The problem of finding a maximum matching in a bipartite graph has many practical applications. As an example, we might consider matching a set L of machines with a set R of tasks to be performed simultaneously. We take the presence of edge .u; _x0017_/ in E to mean that a particular machine u 2 L is capable of performing a particular task _x0017_ 2 R. Jarvis’s march computes the convex hull of a set Q of points by a technique known as package wrapping (or gift wrapping). The algorithm runs in time O.nh/, where h is the number of vertices of CH.Q/. When h is o.lg n/, Jarvis’s march is asymptotically faster than Graham’s scan. Intuitively, Jarvis’s march simulates wrapping a taut piece of paper around the set Q. We start by taping the end of the paper to the lowest point in the set, that is, to the same point p0 with which we start Graham’s scan. We know that this point must be a vertex of the convex hull. We pull the paper to the right to make it taut, and then we pull it higher until it touches a point. This point must also be a vertex of the convex hull. Keeping the paper taut, we continue in this way around the set of vertices until we come back to our original point p0. More formally, Jarvis’s march builds a sequence H D hp0; p1; : : : ; ph1i of the vertices of CH.Q/. We start with p0. As Figure 33.9 shows, the next vertex p1 in the convex hull has the smallest polar angle with respect to p0. (In case of ties, we choose the point farthest from p0.) Similarly, p2 has the smallest polar angle with respect to p1, and so on. When we reach the highest vertex, say pk (breaking
ties by choosing the farthest such vertex), we have constructed, as Figure 33.9
shows, the right chain of CH.Q/. To construct the left chain, we start at pk and
choose pkC1 as the point with the smallest polar angle with respect to pk, but from
the negative x-axis. We continue on, forming the left chain by taking polar angles
from the negative x-axis, until we come back to our original vertex p0.
We could implement Jarvis’s march in one conceptual sweep around the convex
hull, that is, without separately constructing the right and left chains. Such implementations typically keep track of the angle of the last convex-hull side chosen and
require the sequence of angles of hull sides to be strictly increasing (in the range
of 0 to 2_x0019_ radians). The advantage of constructing separate chains is that we need
not explicitly compute angles; the techniques of Section 33.1 suffice to compare
angles.
If implemented properly, Jarvis’s march has a running time of O.nh/. For each
of the h vertices of CH.Q/, we find the vertex with the minimum polar angle. Each
comparison between polar angles takes O.1/ time, using the techniques of Section 33.1. As Section 9.1 shows, we can compute the minimum of n values in O.n/
time if each comparison takes O.1/ time. Thus, Jarvis’s march takes O.nh/ time.

Then, we construct the left chain by finding smallest polar angles with respect to the negative x-axis.

Bucket sort assumes that the input is drawn from a uniform distribution and has an average-case running time of O.n/. Like counting sort, bucket sort is fast because it assumes something about the input. Whereas counting sort assumes that the input consists of integers in a small range, bucket sort assumes that the input is generated by a random process that distributes elements uniformly and independently over the interval Œ0; 1/. (See Section C.2 for a definition of uniform distribution.) Bucket sort divides the interval Œ0; 1/ into n equal-sized subintervals, or buckets, and then distributes the n input numbers into the buckets. Since the inputs are uniformly and independently distributed over Œ0; 1/, we do not expect many numbers to fall into each bucket. To produce the output, we simply sort the numbers in each bucket and then go through the buckets in order, listing the elements in each. context: We now examine a selection algorithm whose running time is O.n/ in the worst case. Like RANDOMIZED-SELECT, the algorithm SELECT finds the desired element by recursively partitioning the input array. Here, however, we guarantee a good split upon partitioning the array. SELECT uses the deterministic partitioning algorithm PARTITION from quicksort (see Section 7.1), but modified to take the element to partition around as an input parameter. The SELECT algorithm determines the ith smallest of an input array of n > 1 distinct elements by executing the following steps. (If n D 1, then SELECT merely returns its only input value as the ith smallest.) 1. Divide the n elements of the input array into bn=5c groups of 5 elements each and at most one group made up of the remaining n mod 5 elements. 2. Find the median of each of the dn=5e groups by first insertion-sorting the elements of each group (of which there are at most 5) and then picking the median from the sorted list of group elements. 3. Use SELECT recursively to find the median x of the dn=5e medians found in step 2. (If there are an even number of medians, then by our convention, x is the lower median.) 4. Partition the input array around the median-of-medians x using the modified version of PARTITION. Let k be one more than the number of elements on the low side of the partition, so that x is the kth smallest element and there are nk elements on the high side of the partition. 5. If i D k, then return x. Otherwise, use SELECT recursively to find the ith smallest element on the low side if i < k, or the .i k/th smallest element on the high side if i > k. To analyze the running time of SELECT, we first determine a lower bound on the number of elements that are greater than the partitioning element x. Figure 9.1 helps us to visualize this bookkeeping.
caption: Analysis of the algorithm SELECT. The n elements are represented by small circles, and each group of 5 elements occupies a column. The medians of the groups are whitened, and the median-of-medians x is labeled. (When finding the median of an even number of elements, we use the lower median.) Arrows go from larger elements to smaller, from which we can see that 3 out of every full group of 5 elements to the right of x are greater than x, and 3 out of every group of 5 elements to the left of x are less than x. The elements known to be greater than x appear on a shaded background.

The Barber-pole illusion is an illustration of the aperture problem. The barber pole induces the illusion of downward motion while rotating.

### Representation of Optical Flow

In the section, we described neural nets as being a
sequence of mappings from raw data to ever more abstracted
representations, layer by layer. This perspective puts representation
learning in the spotlight: deep learning is just representation
learning! Let us now point out an alternative perspective: in backward
order, deep nets are mappings from abstracted representations to ever

context:
What if our data and activations are high-dimensional? The plots above only can visualize 1D and 2D data distributions. Deep representations are typically much higher-dimensional than this, and to visualize them, we need to apply tools from dimensionality reduction. These tools project the high-dimensional data to a lower dimensionality, for example 2D, which can be visualized. A common objective is to perform the projection such that the distance between two datapoints in the 2D projection is roughly proportional to their actual distance in the high-dimensional space. In the next plot, the figure, we use a dimensionality reduction technique called t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding. t-SNE ~\cite{tsne} to visualize how different layers of a modern deep net represent a dataset of images of different semantic classes, where each color represents a different semantic class. The network we are visualizing is of the transformer architecture, and we will learn about all its details in the section. For now, the important things to note are that (1) we are only showing a selected few of the layers (this net actually has dozen of layers) and (2) the embeddings are high-dimensional (in particular, they are 38,400-dimensional) but mapped down to 2D by t-SNE. Therefore, this visualization is just a rough view of what is going on in the net, unlike the visualizations in the previous section, which showed the exact embeddings and every single step of the layer-to-layer transformations.

How a powerful deep net remaps input images into a disentangled representation where semantic classes (shown in different colors) are separated. This deep net is a vision transformer (ViT~\cite{dosovitskiy2020vit}), which we will learn about in \sect{\ref{sec:transformers:ViT_arch}}. It was trained using contrastive language-image pre-training (CLIP~\cite{radford2021learning}, see \sect{\ref{sec:VLMs:CLIP}}). Each `ViT block` contains multiple layers of neural processing (see \fig{\ref{fig-transformers-ViT_arch}}; we visualize the embeddings right after the first `token norm` in a block). We apply t-SNE jointly across all shown layers.
caption: How a powerful deep net remaps input images into a disentangled representation where semantic classes (shown in different colors) are separated. This deep net is a vision transformer (ViT~\cite{dosovitskiy2020vit}), which we will learn about in \sect{\ref{sec:transformers:ViT_arch}}. It was trained using contrastive language-image pre-training (CLIP~\cite{radford2021learning}, see \sect{\ref{sec:VLMs:CLIP}}). Each `ViT block` contains multiple layers of neural processing (see \fig{\ref{fig-transformers-ViT_arch}}; we visualize the embeddings right after the first `token norm` in a block). We apply t-SNE jointly across all shown layers.
input prompt: This figure tracks a dataset's representation through a vision transformer as a vertical stack of five flat square planes in isometric perspective, with an architecture legend up the left side. The legend alternates upward-pointing arrows with four rounded boxes, each reading ViT block x3, so consecutive planes are separated by three transformer blocks. Every plane carries the same set of plotted points, each colored by its semantic class in roughly ten hues including teal, blue, olive, green, orange, red, brown, purple, and pink. Dashed curves in matching colors connect each point to its counterpart on the plane above, so one image can be followed through the whole stack. On the bottom plane the colors are thoroughly mixed within a narrow band; the middle planes remain largely intermingled; and by the top plane the points have spread out into separate compact clumps, each a single color. Position encodes the projected embedding and color encodes class, so what the reader compares plane to plane is how tangled the colors are. The coordinates come from a t-SNE projection computed jointly across the layers shown, giving a rough view of how depth disentangles the classes.
interactions:
- Slider for network depth; the learner moves from the bottom embedding plane to the top plane, the colored point clouds update layer by layer, and it becomes clear how ViT blocks gradually untangle semantic classes.
- Hover over a class color; the learner hovers a colored cluster, matching points and dashed paths brighten across every plane, and the relationship between one semantic class and its representation trajectory becomes clear.
- Button/state for stepping through ViT block groups; the learner advances one ViT block x3 stage at a time, the corresponding plane and incoming paths highlight, and it becomes clear that separation accumulates across repeated transformer blocks.

context:
The graph of a quadratic function is a U-shaped curve called a parabola. One important feature of the graph is that it has an extreme point, called the vertex. If the parabola opens up, the vertex represents the lowest point on the graph, or the minimum value of the quadratic function. If the parabola opens down, the vertex represents the highest point on the graph, or the maximum value. In either case, the vertex is a turning point on the graph. The graph is also symmetric with a vertical line drawn through the vertex, called the axis of symmetry. These features are illustrated in the figure.

Graph of a parabola showing where the x and y intercepts, vertex, and axis of symmetry are.

The y-intercept is the point at which the parabola crosses the y-axis. The x-intercepts are the points at which the parabola crosses the x-axis. If they exist, the x-intercepts represent the zeros, or roots, of the quadratic function, the values of x at which y=0.
source: OpenStax Precalculus 2e, chapter 3: Polynomial and Rational Functions

The curve is a heavy teal U with arrowheads on both rising branches; its lowest point sits at x equal to 1, y equal to -4, and the branches climb to about y equal to 5 near x equal to -2 on the left and x equal to 4 on the right. Small filled dots mark the two crossings of the x-axis at x equal to -1 and x equal to 3, the crossing of the y-axis at y equal to -3, the turning point, and the mirror partner of the y-intercept at x equal to 2. A red dashed vertical line runs through x equal to 1, reached by an arrow from the label Axis of symmetry above. Three further labels point to the graph and read x-intercepts, y-intercept, and Vertex. Drawing the dashed line through the turning point lets the reader check that the marked dots sit at equal heights on either side. The graph fixes the vocabulary for reading a quadratic.

input prompt: This figure consists of one large unit circle annotated with the standard special angles and the coordinates of their terminal points. A heavy black circle is centered on thin horizontal and vertical axes, and sixteen straight radii run from the center out to filled dots placed every 30 or 45 degrees around the circumference. Each dot carries an external label in two colors: the angle written in degrees and then in radians in red, followed by the point's (x, y) coordinates in black. Reading counterclockwise from the right, the labels begin 0 degrees, 0, (1, 0), with 360 degrees, 2pi, (1, 0) printed directly beneath it, then 30 degrees, pi/6, (sqrt(3)/2, 1/2); 45 degrees, pi/4, (sqrt(2)/2, sqrt(2)/2); 60 degrees, pi/3, (1/2, sqrt(3)/2); and 90 degrees, pi/2, (0, 1) at the top. The second quadrant continues with 120, 135, and 150 degrees and closes at 180 degrees, pi, (-1, 0); the third runs 210, 225, and 240 degrees to 270 degrees, 3pi/2, (0, -1); and the fourth returns through 300 and 315 degrees to 330 degrees, 11pi/6, (sqrt(3)/2, -1/2). The symmetric placement is the point of the layout, since the same three magnitudes 1/2, sqrt(2)/2, and sqrt(3)/2 recur in every quadrant with only their signs changing. From the right end of that base a vertical side rises, labeled p on its outer edge. The hypotenuse slants down from the top of the vertical side to the left vertex, labeled h above its middle. A small open square at the lower right vertex marks the right angle between the base and the vertical side, and a single arc at the left vertex marks the acute angle, labeled with the Greek letter theta. The labeling is organized around theta rather than around the page: a is adjacent to theta, p is opposite it, and h is the hypotenuse, so each name states a role rather than a direction. Carrying no numbers at all, the drawing serves as the reference diagram for recovering an unknown acute angle from two known side lengths, the given pair determining which inverse trigonometric relation applies.

context:
Oblique triangles in the category SSA may have four different outcomes. The figure illustrates the solutions with the known sides a and b and known angle α.

Four attempted oblique triangles are in a row, all with standard labels. Side c is the horizontal base. In the first attempted triangle, side a is less than the altitude height. Since side a cannot reach side c, there is no triangle. In the second attempted triangle, side a is equal to the length of the altitude height, so side a forms a right angle with side c. In the third attempted triangle, side a is greater than the altitude height and less than side b, so side a can form either an acute or obtuse angle with side c. In the fourth attempted triangle, side a is greater than or equal to side b, so side a forms an acute angle with side c.
source: OpenStax Precalculus 2e, chapter 8: Further Applications of Trigonometry
input prompt: This figure sets four triangle sketches in a row, labeled (a) through (d) below, to enumerate the possible outcomes when two sides and a non-included angle are known. All four share one labeling scheme: an acute angle alpha marked by an arc at the left end of a horizontal base, a vertex beta at the right end of that base, an apex gamma above, side b rising from alpha to gamma, and side a hanging from gamma. Panel (a), headed No triangle, a < h, draws a as a short vertical segment from gamma that stops above the base, leaving a visible gap so nothing closes. Panel (b), headed Right triangle, a = h, has a reaching the base exactly at beta, with a small square marking the right angle formed there. Panel (c), headed Two triangles, a > h, a < b, shows a solid vertical altitude labeled h from gamma to the base, plus two dashed segments each labeled a running from gamma to different landing points, one to the left of the altitude's foot and one at beta. Panel (d), headed One triangle, a is greater than or equal to b, shows a broad triangle whose side a slopes from gamma down to beta. Aligning the four under identical labels isolates the one quantity that changes, the length of a measured against the altitude and against b, and shows how many closures each case admits.

Observing the two triangles in the figure, one acute and one obtuse, we can drop a perpendicular to represent the height and then apply the trigonometric property sinα= opposite hypotenuse to write an equation for area in oblique triangles. In the acute triangle, we have sinα= h c or csinα=h. However, in the obtuse triangle, we drop the perpendicular outside the triangle and extend the base b to form a right triangle. The angle used in calculation is α ′, or 180−α.

Graph of two rose curves side by side. (A) is r=acos(ntheta), where n is even. Eight petals extending from origin, equally spaced. (B) is r=asin(ntheta) where n is odd. Three petals extending from the origin, equally spaced.

input prompt: This figure shows two rose curves plotted on separate polar grids, set side by side and labeled (a) and (b) beneath. Each grid is built from dotted concentric circles crossed by dotted radial spokes, with solid horizontal and vertical axes arrowed at all four ends. Panel (a) holds a teal curve of eight identical petals, all springing from the origin at equal angular intervals so that four lie along the axes and four along the diagonals between them; its caption reads r = acos(n theta), n even. Panel (b) holds a curve in the same teal weight but with only three petals, one pointing straight down along the negative vertical axis and the other two angled up to the left and up to the right, spaced a third of a turn apart; its caption reads r = asin(n theta), n odd. Every petal reaches out to roughly the same radius, so each curve fills a circular envelope. Setting the panels side by side isolates the parity of n as the only thing governing the count: an even n produces 2n petals while an odd n produces just n, and the eight-petal and three-petal drawings are the two cases of that rule.

context:
Vector subtraction is similar to vector addition. To find u − v, view it as u + (−v). Adding −v is reversing direction of v and adding it to the end of u. The new vector begins at the start of u and stops at the end point of −v. See the figure for a visual that compares vector addition and vector subtraction using parallelograms.

Showing vector addition and subtraction with parallelograms. For addition, the base is u, the side is v, the diagonal connecting the start of the base to the end of the side is u+v. For subtraction, thetop is u, the side is -v, and the diagonal connecting the start of the top to the end of the side is u-v.
source: OpenStax Precalculus 2e, chapter 8: Further Applications of Trigonometry
input prompt: This figure sets two congruent parallelograms side by side, outlined in dark blue with both diagonals drawn as thin lines, to place vector addition next to vector subtraction. In the left parallelogram the bottom edge carries an orange arrowhead pointing right and is labeled u; the slanted right-hand edge carries an orange arrowhead pointing up and to the right and is labeled v; and the diagonal running from the lower-left corner to the upper-right corner ends in an orange arrowhead and is labeled u + v. context:
Every ellipse has two axes of symmetry. The longer axis is called the major axis, and the shorter axis is called the minor axis. Each endpoint of the major axis is the vertex of the ellipse (plural: vertices), and each endpoint of the minor axis is a co-vertex of the ellipse. The center of an ellipse is the midpoint of both the major and minor axes. The axes are perpendicular at the center. The foci always lie on the major axis, and the sum of the distances from the foci to any point on the ellipse (the constant sum) is greater than the distance between the foci. See the figure.

A horizontal ellipse centered at (0, 0) in the x y coordinate system, with Major and Minor Axes, Vertices and Co-Vertices, Foci, and Center labeled.

In this section, we restrict ellipses to those that are positioned vertically or horizontally in the coordinate plane. That is, the axes will either lie on or be parallel to the x- and y-axes. Later in the chapter, we will see ellipses that are rotated in the coordinate plane.

A red dashed segment lies along the horizontal axis and spans the full width of the curve; the words "Major Axis" sit below its left half, and its two endpoints, where the outline meets the horizontal axis, are marked with dots and labeled "Vertex" at each end. A second red dashed segment lies along the vertical axis and spans the height of the curve, labeled "Minor Axis" beside its upper half, with black dots at its ends labeled "Co-vertex" above and "Co-vertex" below. The black dot where the two dashed segments cross is labeled "Center." Two small green dots sit on the horizontal dashed segment, one on either side of the center and well inside the vertices, each labeled "Focus." Collecting every named part on a single outline lets the reader tie each term to a definite position relative to the center. The diagram supplies the vocabulary needed to set up and read the standard equation of an ellipse.
interactions:
- Slider for semi-major axis a: the learner drags the horizontal radius, the vertices and major axis stretch while the center stays fixed, and a controls the ellipse's width.
- Slider for semi-minor axis b: the learner drags the vertical radius, the co-vertices and minor axis move while the horizontal vertices stay fixed, and b controls the ellipse's height.
- Toggle between feature labels and equation parameters: the learner switches from center, vertices, co-vertices, and foci labels to a, b, and c distances, showing how the named parts map onto the standard ellipse equation.

context:
As with the ellipse, every hyperbola has two axes of symmetry. The transverse axis is a line segment that passes through the center of the hyperbola and has vertices as its endpoints. The foci lie on the line that contains the transverse axis. The conjugate axis is perpendicular to the transverse axis and has the co-vertices as its endpoints. The center of a hyperbola is the midpoint of both the transverse and conjugate axes, where they intersect. Every hyperbola also has two asymptotes that pass through its center. As a hyperbola recedes from the center, its branches approach these asymptotes. The central rectangle of the hyperbola is centered at the origin with sides that pass through each vertex and co-vertex; it is a useful tool for graphing the hyperbola and its asymptotes. To sketch the asymptotes of the hyperbola, simply sketch and extend the diagonals of the central rectangle. See the figure.

Key features of the hyperbola

This diagram illustrates the various components of a hyperbola centered at the origin, including the vertices, co-vertices, foci, transverse axis, conjugate axis, asymptotes, and the rectangular box used to construct the asymptotes.

In this section, we will limit our discussion to hyperbolas that are positioned vertically or horizontally in the coordinate plane; the axes will either lie on or be parallel to the x- and y-axes. We will consider two cases: those that are centered at the origin, and those that are centered at a point other than the origin.
caption: Key features of the hyperbola

context:
In Quadratic Functions, we learned about a parabola’s vertex and axis of symmetry. Now we extend the discussion to include other key features of the parabola. See the figure. Notice that the axis of symmetry passes through the focus and vertex and is perpendicular to the directrix. The vertex is the midpoint between the directrix and the focus.

The line segment that passes through the focus and is parallel to the directrix is called the latus rectum. The endpoints of the latus rectum lie on the curve. By definition, the distance d from the focus to any point P on the parabola is equal to the distance from P to the directrix.

Key features of the parabola

This image displays a parabola on a Cartesian coordinate plane, clearly labeling its fundamental geometric elements. The blue curve represents the parabola itself. The "Vertex" is indicated as the turning point of the parabola. Inside the curve, the "Focus" is marked, a critical point for defining the parabola. A dashed orange line, labeled "Axis of symmetry", passes vertically through both the vertex and the focus. Below the vertex, a horizontal dashed red line shows the "Directrix". Finally, a horizontal dashed blue line segment passing through the focus and extending to the parabola is identified as the "Latus rectum".

To work with parabolas in the coordinate plane, we consider two cases: those with a vertex at the origin and those with a vertex at a point other than the origin. We begin with the former.
caption: Key features of the parabola

Directly above the vertex on that same vertical line sits a small teal dot labeled Focus in teal. The drawing establishes the vocabulary used to define a parabola as the set of points equally distant from the focus and the directrix.

context:
Until now, we have looked at equations of conic sections without an xy term, which aligns the graphs with the x- and y-axes. When we add an xy term, we are rotating the conic about the origin. If the x- and y-axes are rotated through an angle, say θ, then every point on the plane may be thought of as having two representations: (x,y) on the Cartesian plane with the original x-axis and y-axis, and (x ′, y ′) on the new plane defined by the new, rotated axes, called the x'-axis and y'-axis. See the figure.

The graph of the rotated ellipse x 2 + y 2 –xy–15=0

An ellipse centered at the origin, aligned with a rotated coordinate system (x', y') that is at an angle θ with respect to the standard (x, y) coordinate system.

We will find the relationships between x and y on the Cartesian plane with x ′ and y ′ on the new rotated plane. See the figure.
caption: The graph of the rotated ellipse x 2 + y 2 –xy–15=0
input prompt: This figure is a plane diagram in which one ellipse is shown against two superimposed coordinate systems. The standard frame consists of thin black double-headed arrows, a horizontal axis labeled x at its right end and a vertical axis labeled y at its top, meeting at the origin. Laid over them is a second pair of orange double-headed axes rotated counterclockwise about that same origin: the one running from lower left to upper right is labeled x', and the one running from lower right to upper left is labeled y'. The ellipse is a dark blue outline centered at the origin and tilted so that its long axis lies along the orange x'-axis and its short axis along the y'-axis; it crosses the black horizontal axis on both sides and extends above and below the black vertical axis. A small curved arc drawn between the positive x-axis and the positive x'-axis marks the rotation and is labeled theta. Neither set of axes carries tick marks or numeric values. Placing both frames on one picture invites a comparison between a point's coordinates in the original system and its coordinates in the rotated one. The figure motivates the treatment of conic equations that contain an xy term, which describe conics turned away from alignment with the coordinate axes.
interactions:
- Slider for rotating the coordinate frame by theta: the learner drags theta, the orange x' and y' axes turn with the ellipse while the black x and y axes stay fixed, showing how rotation removes the visual misalignment behind an xy term.
- Toggle between original and rotated equations: the learner switches from the x,y equation with the xy term to the x',y' equation aligned to the ellipse, and the active axes and equation terms highlight together to show why the rotated frame simplifies the conic.
- Click for coordinate comparison at a point: the learner clicks a point on the ellipse, projections to both axis systems appear with two coordinate readouts, making clear that the same point has different coordinates in the two frames.

context:
In two dimensions, the coordinate axes partition the plane into four quadrants. Similarly, the coordinate planes divide space between them into eight regions about the origin, called octants. The octants fill ℝ3 in the same way that quadrants fill ℝ2, as shown in the figure.

Points that lie in octants have three nonzero coordinates.

This figure is the 3-dimensional coordinate system with the first octant labeled with a roman numeral I, I, II, III, IV, V, VI, VII, and VIII. Also, for each quadrant there are the signs of the values of x, y, and z. They are: I (+, +, +); 2nd (-, +, +); 3rd (-, -, +); 4th (+, -, +); 5th (+, +, -); 6th (-, +, -); 7th (-, -, -); and 8th (+, -, -).

Most work in three-dimensional space is a comfortable extension of the corresponding concepts in two dimensions. In this section, we use our knowledge of circles to describe spheres, then we expand our understanding of vectors to three dimensions. To accomplish these goals, we begin by adapting the distance formula to three-dimensional space.
caption: Points that lie in octants have three nonzero coordinates.
source: OpenStax Calculus, chapter 12: Vectors in Space

context:
In the spherical coordinate system, a point P in space (the figure) is represented by the ordered triple (ρ,θ,φ) where

In the Cartesian coordinate system, the location of a point in space is described using an ordered triple in which each coordinate represents a distance. In the cylindrical coordinate system, location of a point in space is described using two distances (randz) and an angle measure (θ). In the spherical coordinate system, we again use an ordered triple to describe the location of a point in space. In this case, the triple describes one distance and two angles. Spherical coordinates make it simple to describe a sphere, just as cylindrical coordinates make it easy to describe a cylinder. Grid lines for spherical coordinates are based on angle measures, like those for polar coordinates.

The relationship among spherical, rectangular, and cylindrical coordinates.

This figure is the first quadrant of the 3-dimensional coordinate system. It has a point labeled “(x, y, z) = (rho, theta, phi).” There is a line segment from the origin to the point. It is labeled “rho.” The angle between this line segment and the z-axis is phi. There is a line segment in the x y-plane from the origin to the shadow of the point. This segment is labeled “r.” The angle between the x-axis and r is theta.

By convention, the origin is represented as (0,0,0) in spherical coordinates.
caption: The relationship among spherical, rectangular, and cylindrical coordinates.
source: OpenStax Calculus, chapter 12: Vectors in Space

As mentioned, the name of the shape of the curve of the graph in the examplec. is a helix (the figure). The curve resembles a spring, with a circular cross-section looking down along the z-axis. It is possible for a helix to be elliptical in cross-section as well. For example, the vector-valued function r(t)=4costi+3sintj+tk describes an elliptical helix. The projection of this helix into the x,y-plane is an ellipse. Last, the arrows in the graph of this helix indicate the orientation of the curve as t progresses from 0 to 4π.

The graph of the third vector-valued function is a helix.

This figure is the graph of a helix in the 3 dimensional coordinate system. The curve represents the function r(t) = cost i + sint j + tk. The curve spirals in a circular path around the vertical z-axis and has the look of a spring. The arrows on the curve represent orientation.
caption: The graph of the third vector-valued function is a helix.

Two arrowheads placed on the ascending curve show the direction of travel. Across the upper right, in bold, the formula r(t) = 4cost i + 4sint j + t k is printed. Holding the loop radius constant while the height grows in step with the parameter is precisely what produces the spring-like shape. context:
Let P0=(x0,y0,z0) be a point on a surface S, and let C be any curve passing through P0 and lying entirely in S. If the tangent lines to all such curves C at P0 lie in the same plane, then this plane is called the tangent plane to S at P0 (the figure).

Intuitively, it seems clear that, in a plane, only one line can be tangent to a curve at a point. However, in three-dimensional space, many lines can be tangent to a given point. If these lines lie in the same plane, they determine the tangent plane at that point. A tangent plane at a regular point contains all of the lines tangent to that point. A more intuitive way to think of a tangent plane is to assume the surface is smooth at that point (no corners). Then, a tangent line to the surface at that point in any direction does not have any abrupt changes in slope because the direction changes smoothly.

The tangent plane to a surface S at a point P0 contains all the tangent lines to curves in S that pass through P0.

A surface S is shown with a point P0 = (x0, y0, z0). There are two intersecting curves shown on S that pass through P0. There are tangents drawn for each of these curves at P0, and these tangent lines create a plane, namely, the tangent plane at P0.

For a tangent plane to a surface to exist at a point on that surface, it is sufficient for the function that defines the surface to be differentiable at that point, defined later in this section. We define the term tangent plane here and then explore the idea intuitively.
caption: The tangent plane to a surface S at a point P0 contains all the tangent lines to curves in S that pass through P0.
source: OpenStax Calculus, chapter 14: Differentiation of Functions of Several Variables
