context:
Suppose the function z=f(x,y) is differentiable at (x0,y0) (the figure).

The ‖u‖ disappears because u is a unit vector. Therefore, the directional derivative is equal to the magnitude of the gradient evaluated at (x0,y0) multiplied by cosφ. Recall that cosφ ranges from −1 to 1. If φ=0, then cosφ=1 and ∇f(x0,y0) and u both point in the same direction. If φ=π, then cosφ=−1 and ∇f(x0,y0) and u point in opposite directions. In the first case, the value of Duf(x0,y0) is maximized; in the second case, the value of Duf(x0,y0) is minimized. If ∇f(x0,y0)=0, then Duf(x0,y0)=∇f(x0,y0)·u=0 for any vector u. These three cases are outlined in the following theorem.

The gradient indicates the maximum and minimum values of the directional derivative at a point.

An upward facing paraboloid in xyz space with point P0 (x0, y0, z0). From this point, there are arrows going up, down, and around the paraboloid. On the xy plane, the point (x0, y0) is marked, and the corresponding arrows are drawn onto the plane: the down arrow corresponds to −∇f (most rapid decrease in f), the up arrow corresponds to ∇f (most rapid increase in f), and the arrows around correspond to no change in f. The up/down arrows are perpendicular to the around arrows in their projection on the plane.

The figure shows a portion of the graph of the function f(x,y)=3+sinxsiny. Given a point (a,b) in the domain of f, the maximum value of the gradient at that point is given by ‖∇f(a,b)‖. This would equal the rate of greatest ascent if the surface represented a topographical map. If we went in the opposite direction, it would be the rate of greatest descent.
caption: The gradient indicates the maximum and minimum values of the directional derivative at a point.
source: OpenStax Calculus, chapter 14: Differentiation of Functions of Several Variables

context:
Now we can illustrate the following theorem for triple integrals in spherical coordinates with (ρijk*,θijk*,φijk*) being any sample point in the spherical subbox Bijk. For the volume element of the subbox ΔV in spherical coordinates, we have ΔV=(Δρ)(ρΔφ)(ρsinφΔθ),, as shown in the following figure.

The volume element of a box in spherical coordinates.

In the spherical coordinate space, a box is projected onto the polar coordinate plane. On the polar coordinate plane, the projection has area rho sin phi Delta theta. On the z axis, a distance Delta rho is indicated, and from these boundaries, angles are made that project through the edges of the box. There is also a blown up version of the box that shows it has sides Delta rho, rho Delta phi, and rho sin phi Delta theta, with overall volume Delta V = rho squared sin phi Delta rho Delta phi Delta theta.

As with the other multiple integrals we have examined, all the properties work similarly for a triple integral in the spherical coordinate system, and so do the iterated integrals. Fubini’s theorem takes the following form.
caption: The volume element of a box in spherical coordinates.

On the left, x, y, and z axes radiate from a common origin and a small curved orange box floats above the first octant, bounded by two dashed circular arcs of slightly different radii and by dashed rays fanning out from the origin. A bracket on the z axis marks the radial increment Delta rho, the angular gap between the two rays reaching the box is marked Delta phi, and a small angle in the horizontal plane near the origin is marked Delta theta. A flat blue quadrilateral in the xy-plane is the projection of the box, with a bracket beneath labeled rho sin phi and an arrow into it labeled rho sin phi Delta theta. A thick gray curved arrow sweeps right to an enlarged copy of the same box, whose three edges are labeled Delta rho, rho Delta phi, and rho sin phi Delta theta, with Delta V = rho^2 sin phi Delta rho Delta phi Delta theta printed below. Showing the subbox in place and again blown up lets each edge be matched to the coordinate increment that generates it. The construction motivates the factor rho^2 sin phi that appears when a triple integral is rewritten in spherical coordinates.
interactions:
- Slider for Delta rho, Delta phi, and Delta theta: the learner drags each increment and the orange spherical subbox plus its magnified inset stretch along the matching edge, making clear how the three coordinate increments multiply into Delta V.
- Toggle between in-place and enlarged element labels: the learner switches label overlays on the coordinate diagram and the inset, and the same edge is highlighted in both locations, making clear why rho Delta phi and rho sin phi Delta theta are arc-length factors rather than raw angle measures.

input prompt: This figure is a three-dimensional vector field plot drawn inside a light blue wireframe cube, with black x, y, and z axes running through it; x points toward the lower left, y to the right, and z vertically. A small shaded blue sphere sits where the axes cross, marked with the label 0, standing for a large mass at the origin. Arrows fill the interior of the cube and every one points inward toward that sphere. Those closest to the origin are long and bright orange, those at intermediate distance shorter and teal, and those near the corners and faces reduced to small dashes, so length and color together carry the magnitude of the field. Several of the longest arrows lie along the axis directions and meet the sphere head on. Because length and direction vary independently, the reader takes in both at once: the field aims at the central mass everywhere, and its strength climbs sharply as distance to the origin shrinks. The plot renders the gravitational field of a point mass, making visible the uniformly attractive radial direction and the rapid growth in magnitude near the source.

input prompt: This figure shows an oriented surface sitting inside a three-dimensional vector field, drawn within a thin blue wireframe box whose x, y, and z axes carry evenly spaced tick marks; x heads toward the lower left, y toward the lower right, and z upward. The surface is a thick blue-gray tube that winds and doubles back through the middle of the box, its lobes passing both in front of and behind the z axis so the shape overlaps itself. context:
Let S be a piecewise, smooth closed surface that encloses solid E in space. Assume that S is oriented outward, and let F be a vector field with continuous partial derivatives on an open region containing E (the figure). Then

The divergence theorem follows the general pattern of these other theorems. If we think of divergence as a derivative of sorts, then the divergence theorem relates a triple integral of derivative divF over a solid to a flux integral of F over the boundary of the solid. More specifically, the divergence theorem relates a flux integral of vector field F over a closed surface S to a triple integral of the divergence of F over the solid enclosed by S.

The divergence theorem relates a flux integral across a closed surface S to a triple integral over solid E enclosed by the surface.

A diagram of a closed surface S, vector field, and solid E enclosed by the surface in three dimensions. The surface is a roughly rectangular prism with curved sides. The normal vectors stretch out and away from the surface. The arrows have negative x components and positive y and z components.

Recall that the flux form of Green’s theorem states that ∬DdivFdA=∫CF·Nds. Therefore, the divergence theorem is a version of Green’s theorem in one higher dimension.
caption: The divergence theorem relates a flux integral across a closed surface S to a triple integral over solid E enclosed by the surface.
input prompt: This figure is a single three-dimensional diagram of a closed surface carrying outward normal vectors. A pale blue solid shaped like a rectangular prism with bulging faces and rounded edges occupies the center, set in a frame whose z axis rises at the upper left, y axis extends right, and x axis comes forward to the lower left. The letter E labels the solid at its middle and the letter S labels the boundary near its upper right. Short dark blue arrows, each labeled N, project outward from the boundary: two from the top, two from the bottom, one from the left face, one from the right face, and one drawn on the upper surface angling up and back. Longer unlabeled orange arrows run in parallel through and around the figure from lower left to upper right, standing for the ambient vector field. Dashed curves mark the hidden rear edges. Setting the labeled normals against the uniformly directed field arrows shows at a glance how much of the field crosses the boundary at each face. The diagram accompanies a result tying the flux of a vector field across a closed surface to a triple integral of its divergence over the solid inside.
interactions:
- Click for each face region of S: the learner selects a patch of the closed surface and the outward normal N and nearby orange field arrows brighten, making clear when the field contributes positive, negative, or little flux through that patch.
- Toggle between boundary-flux and enclosed-volume views: the learner switches emphasis from arrows crossing S to shading inside E, making clear that the divergence theorem equates surface flux with accumulation of divergence throughout the solid.

input prompt: This figure is a plain black line drawing of a right circular cylinder viewed in perspective from slightly above. The top face is rendered as a complete ellipse; the bottom is a partial ellipse whose far arc is omitted, and the two are joined by straight vertical lines at the left and right silhouette edges, so the solid reads as opaque. context:
Many real-world situations can be represented by ellipses, including orbits of planets, satellites, moons and comets, and shapes of boat keels, rudders, and some airplane wings. A medical device called a lithotripter uses elliptical reflectors to break up kidney stones by generating sound waves. Some buildings, called whispering chambers, are designed with elliptical domes so that a person whispering at one focus can easily be heard by someone standing at the other focus. This occurs because of the acoustic properties of an ellipse. When a sound wave originates at one focus of a whispering chamber, the sound wave will be reflected off the elliptical dome and back to the other focus. See the figure. In the whisper chamber at the Museum of Science and Industry in Chicago, two people standing at the foci—about 43 feet apart—can hear each other whisper. When these chambers are placed in unexpected places, such as the ones inside Bush International Airport in Houston and Grand Central Terminal in New York City, they can induce surprised reactions among travelers.

Sound waves are reflected between foci in an elliptical room, called a whispering chamber.

An illustration of a semi-ellipsoidal dome with two focal points, F and F'. Blue lines with arrows represent rays originating from focal point F'. These rays reflect off the inner curved surface of the dome and converge at the second focal point F, demonstrating the reflective property of an ellipse.
caption: Sound waves are reflected between foci in an elliptical room, called a whispering chamber.
input prompt: This figure is a shaded three-dimensional cutaway drawing of a domed room built as a half-ellipsoid on a circular base. The outer shell carries a blue-to-white gradient and is cut away at the front so the viewer looks into the interior, where the inner surface and the floor are shaded warm tan; a thick gray band forms the base slab beneath the floor. Two small dark points on the floor mark the foci, labeled F' on the left and F on the right. A fan of dark blue segments with arrowheads leaves F', rises at a range of angles to strike the inside of the curved dome at several separated points, and reflects back down, every one arriving at F. The paths cross one another mid-room, and no two share a bounce point. Drawing many distinct routes between the same pair of labeled points emphasizes that the convergence holds no matter which direction a ray sets out in. The illustration accounts for the acoustics of a whispering chamber, where a person speaking softly at one focus of an elliptical dome is heard clearly by a listener at the other.
interactions:
- Click for an outgoing sound ray from F': the learner selects one path and its reflection point and return segment to F are highlighted, making clear that different launch angles still arrive at the other focus.
- Animation for sound propagation: the learner plays pulses leaving F', bouncing once off the ellipsoidal dome, and converging at F, making clear the dynamic reflection path behind the whispering-chamber effect.
- Toggle between single-ray and all-rays views: the learner switches from one highlighted route to the full fan of reflected paths, making clear that the focus-to-focus property is systematic rather than a coincidence of one ray.

context:
As we have seen, conic sections are formed when a plane intersects two right circular cones aligned tip to tip and extending infinitely far in opposite directions, which we also call a cone. The way in which we slice the cone will determine the type of conic section formed at the intersection. A circle is formed by slicing a cone with a plane perpendicular to the axis of symmetry of the cone. An ellipse is formed by slicing a single cone with a slanted plane not perpendicular to the axis of symmetry. A parabola is formed by slicing the plane through the top or bottom of the double-cone, whereas a hyperbola is formed when the plane slices both the top and bottom of the cone. See the figure.

The nondegenerate conic sections

Different conic sections (ellipse, circle, hyperbola, parabola) formed by intersecting a double cone with a plane at various angles.

Ellipses, circles, hyperbolas, and parabolas are sometimes called the nondegenerate conic sections, in contrast to the degenerate conic sections, which are shown in the figure. A degenerate conic results when a plane intersects the double cone and passes through the apex. Depending on the angle of the plane, three types of degenerate conic sections are possible: a point, a line, or two intersecting lines.
caption: The nondegenerate conic sections
input prompt: This figure is a four-column chart showing how different plane cuts through a double cone produce different curves, with cone drawings across the top row and the resulting curves below. Each cone is drawn identically in pale blue as two nappes meeting point to point, the upper rim a solid blue ellipse and the lower rim a dashed one, and a red curve marks where a cutting plane meets it. The columns are titled Diagonal Slice, Horizontal Slice, Deep Vertical Slice, and Vertical Slice. The first shows a red ellipse tilted across the upper nappe; the second a red ellipse lying level across the upper nappe; the third two red arcs, one curving up through the top nappe and one down through the bottom; the fourth a single red arc cutting downward through the lower nappe only. Below each cone the curve is named and redrawn on its own in red, free of the cone: Ellipse as a flattened oval, Circle as a round closed curve, Hyperbola as two opposing branches, Parabola as a single upward-opening arc. Keeping each slice above its isolated curve lets the angle of the cut be read directly against the shape it yields. The chart sorts the four nondegenerate conic sections by the orientation of the generating plane.
interactions:
- Slider for cutting-plane angle: the learner tilts a plane through a double cone and the red intersection morphs from circle to ellipse to parabola or hyperbola, making clear how plane orientation determines the conic type.
- Toggle between cone slice and isolated curve: the learner switches each column between the 3D cut and the red curve alone, making clear how the visible intersection on the cone becomes the named planar graph.
- Button sequence for the four conics: the learner steps through ellipse, circle, hyperbola, and parabola, and the matching slice plus label is highlighted, making clear the classification of nondegenerate conic sections by slice direction.
